content: Color vision refers to the ability of an organism or a machine to differentiate objects based on the wavelengths of light they reflect or emit. The human nervous system interprets color by comparing the responses of three types of cone photoreceptors in the retina, each sensitive to different parts of the visible spectrum. Humans typically perceive light within the range of 380 to 750 nanometers, and the three types of cones—commonly referred to as S-cones, M-cones, and L-cones—are sensitive to short, medium, and long wavelengths, respectively. The perception of color is not an inherent property of objects but rather a construct of the visual brain. For example, a red apple appears red because it absorbs most wavelengths of visible light except for those perceived as red, which are reflected and detected by the eye. To perceive color, three components are necessary: a light source, a detector (such as the eye), and an object to observe. The advantage of color perception lies in its ability to enhance the discrimination of surfaces, which is critical for animals to interact effectively with their environment. This process involves the interpretation of object forms and colors by the visual system. Physiology of Color Perception In mammals, color perception is mediated by cone photoreceptors containing pigments with distinct spectral sensitivities. Humans and closely related primates possess three types of cones, enabling trichromatic vision. This contrasts with many other mammals, which are dichromats and have limited or no color vision. The L-cones, often associated with red perception, are most sensitive to greenish-yellow light, while M-cones and S-cones are sensitive to green and blue-violet light, respectively. It is important to note that the RGB color model used in technology does not directly correspond to the cone types in the human eye. The peak sensitivity of cone photoreceptors varies among individuals with normal color vision and is even more variable in non-human species, where such polymorphism may confer adaptive advantages. For example, yellowish-green light stimulates both L and M cones strongly but has minimal effect on S-cones. Red light predominantly stimulates L-cones, while blue-green light activates M-cones and S-cones to varying degrees. Violet light primarily stimulates S-cones. The pigments in L and M cones are encoded on the X chromosome, and mutations in these genes can lead to common forms of color blindness. The OPN1LW gene, responsible for the pigment sensitive to yellowish light, is highly polymorphic, with some women possessing an additional cone type, resulting in tetrachromatic vision. Variations in the OPN1MW gene, which encodes the bluish-green pigment, are rare and do not significantly affect spectral sensitivity. Color Processing in the Human Brain Color processing begins in the retina through color-opponent mechanisms, which involve opposing pairs such as red-green, blue-yellow, and light-dark. Visual information is transmitted via the optic nerve to the optic chiasm, where signals from the temporal visual field cross to the opposite side of the brain. The optic tracts then relay this information to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) in the thalamus. The LGN contains six layers, including two achromatic magnocellular layers and four chromatic parvocellular layers. The parvocellular layers process red-green and blue-yellow opponent signals. From the LGN, visual information is sent to the primary visual cortex (V1) in the occipital lobe. In V1, color processing becomes more complex, with some neurons exhibiting color tuning that varies depending on the adaptation state of the visual system. Specialized neurons known as double-opponent cells are thought to play a key role in color vision. These cells, first described in the goldfish retina and later identified in primates, compare local cone ratios and are organized into clusters called blobs within V1. Double-opponent cells are particularly sensitive to local color contrasts, such as red adjacent to green. From V1, color information is transmitted to the second visual area (V2), where color-tuned neurons are concentrated in thin stripes. These neurons project to area V4, a large visual region involved in processing color, shape, and curvature. While V4 was initially thought to be exclusively dedicated to color, it is now understood to have broader functions, including sensitivity to attention and integration of color with shape and form. V4 neurons provide input to the inferior temporal cortex, which is believed to combine color information with object recognition. Color Vision in Other Animals Many animals have more complex color vision systems than humans. For instance, some tropical fish and birds exhibit tetrachromatic vision, with four types of cones. Birds often have brightly colored oil droplets in their cones, which modify spectral sensitivity. Pigeons may even possess pentachromatic vision. In contrast, most mammals are dichromats, and marine mammals are monochromats with only one cone type. Invertebrates also display diverse color vision capabilities. Bees, for example, have trichromatic vision sensitive to ultraviolet light, while butterflies may have tetrachromatic vision despite having six photoreceptor types. Stomatopods, such as mantis shrimp, have the most complex color vision system, with up to 12 spectral receptor types. Evolution of Color Vision The evolution of color vision is closely tied to ecological needs, such as food recognition. For herbivorous primates, color vision aids in identifying ripe fruits and mature leaves. Hummingbirds use color to recognize specific flower types. Nocturnal mammals, on the other hand, have less-developed color vision due to the low light levels required for cone function. Ultraviolet light plays a significant role in the color perception of many insects and other animals. Trichromatic vision evolved in the ancestors of modern primates as they adapted to diurnal activity and fruit consumption. Mathematical Modeling of Color Perception Color perception can be mathematically modeled as a mapping from the infinite-dimensional space of physical colors (Hcolor) to a three-dimensional Euclidean space (R3color). Each physical color is represented as a function of wavelength intensity, while perceived colors correspond to the stimulation of the three cone types. This mapping is linear but not unique, as multiple physical spectra can produce the same perceived color. The resulting combinations form a mathematical cone in three-dimensional space, with cross-sections representing chromaticity. The CIE chromaticity diagram, for example, illustrates the range of perceivable colors, including spectral colors and purples. Chromatic Adaptation and the Von Kries Transform Chromatic adaptation, or color constancy, allows humans to perceive consistent object colors under varying lighting conditions. This phenomenon is achieved through mechanisms such as the von Kries transform, which adjusts the gains of cone responses to maintain the appearance of a reference white. The von Kries transform involves diagonal adaptation matrices that map cone responses between different adaptation states, providing a mathematical framework for understanding color constancy.
